title: Splitting a CSV file into lines first breaks a row that has a quoted newline in it
assumption: Each line of a CSV file is one row, so splitting the file on newlines before parsing fields is safe.

input.description: A CSV export of a notes or address field that contains an embedded newline (a multi-line note, a two-line mailing address) wrapped in quotes, as RFC 4180 requires.

what_goes_wrong: Splitting the raw text into lines first (`text.splitlines()` in Python, `text.split("\n")` in JS) turns one logical two-field row into three separate "lines" - the quoted field's embedded newline is treated as a row boundary before the quoting is ever examined, so no amount of comma-aware parsing afterward can put the row back together.
why: RFC 4180 allows a quoted field to contain literal newline characters as part of its value - a row boundary is only the newline that appears outside a quoted field. A real CSV parser (Python's `csv` module) reads character by character and tracks whether it is currently inside a quote, so it does not treat a newline as a row separator while inside quotes. Pre-splitting the text into lines with `splitlines()`/`split("\n")` throws that context away before the parser ever runs, so the damage is already done.
affects: any CSV handling that splits into lines before parsing fields

repros.code:
import csv, io
text = 'name,note\n"Smith","Line1\nLine2"\n'
print(text.splitlines())
naive = [line.split(",") for line in text.splitlines()]
print(naive)
proper = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text)))
print(proper)

fix: Never split a CSV file into lines before parsing fields. Hand the whole text (or a stream) to a real quote-aware CSV parser - Python's `csv.reader`, or a maintained CSV library in JS - and let it decide where rows actually end.

sources.title: RFC 4180: Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files
Python docs: csv - CSV File Reading and Writing

test_cases.note: A CSV-parsing function given this text must return two rows, with the embedded newline preserved inside the second field's value rather than splitting into three rows.
